grammarChart.title: Passive Voice: be + past participle
grammarChart.structure: Subject + form of 'be' + past participle of the main verb + (optional: by + agent)

tenses.passive: The walls are being painted (by them).
The car was being fixed (by him).
My bike has been stolen (by someone).
The project had been finished (by them).
An invitation will be sent (by us).

tenses.active: She is going to bake a cake.
tenses.passive: A cake is going to be baked (by her).
The task should be completed (by you).

explanation: The passive voice is used when the action or the object of the action is more important than the person or thing performing the action (the agent). It shifts the focus from the doer to the receiver of the action. The structure involves a form of the verb 'to be' (am, is, are, was, were, be, being, been) followed by the past participle of the main verb. The agent (the doer) is often omitted or introduced with the preposition 'by'.
keyRules: Identify the object of the active sentence. This becomes the subject of the passive sentence.
Use the correct form of 'be' according to the tense of the active sentence.
Use the past participle of the main verb.
The agent (the doer) can be included with 'by' or omitted if it is unknown, unimportant, or obvious from the context.
When converting from active to passive, remember that transitive verbs (verbs that take an object) are required.
azarNotes: Think of 'be' as a helper verb that changes its form based on the tense, while the past participle remains constant for a given verb.
The past participle is the third form of a verb (e.g., eat, ate, eaten; write, wrote, written).
Passive voice is common in formal writing, scientific reports, and news articles where objectivity is important.
examples:
Active: The company launched a new product last year. 
Passive: A new product was launched by the company last year.

Active: The students are completing their assignments. 
Passive: Their assignments are being completed by the students.

Active: The government has implemented new policies. 
Passive: New policies have been implemented (by the government).

Active: The chef will prepare the meal. 
Passive: The meal will be prepared by the chef.

Active: Someone must have left the door open. 
Passive: The door must have been left open.
commonMistakes: Using the wrong form of 'be'. (e.g., 'The book is wrote' instead of 'The book was written').
Using the present participle instead of the past participle. (e.g., 'The cake is baking' instead of 'The cake is being baked' or 'The cake was baked').
Incorrectly forming the passive with intransitive verbs (verbs that don't take an object). (e.g., 'He arrived' cannot be made passive).
Forgetting to change the verb tense when converting to passive.
Overusing the passive voice, which can make writing sound indirect or wordy.
ieltsTip: In IELTS Writing Task 1 (Academic), the passive voice is crucial for describing processes and changes. For example, 'Water is heated...' or 'The raw materials are then mixed...'. In Task 2, use it to present information objectively or when the agent is irrelevant. Be mindful of tense consistency.
